summary: Keeper's-house range lights at the south tip of Daufuskie Island, SC (1883 to 1912 or 1922); the house, moved in 1899, is now a museum and winery.

structures.note: Moved in 1899 to the rear beacon's site (LHB FY1899 and FY1900). Museum and gift shop today.
91 ft per LHF. The station record gives 24.7 m. The sources read do not describe the tower after 1899.
Now the Silver Dew Winery building. The nomination says it sits on a concrete pad that once carried the range tower.

access.note: Privately owned. Open to the public as a museum and gift shop; hours change with the seasons, so call ahead. Daufuskie is reached only by boat, and the island has no cars for visitors.

events.note: Range pair completed in 1883 (nomination, front beacon).
Charleston earthquake, 31 August 1886: the dwelling shook; little damage to station structures (LHF).
Storm of 27-28 August 1893: front beacon and station buildings damaged; boathouse and kitchen rolled by the tide and reset.
October 1898 storm damaged the front beacon; the dwelling's foundations were filled and boarded.
Front-beacon structures moved to the rear beacon's site; work completed December 1899 with no interruption of the light.
Front beacon replaced by the iron tower discontinued at Venus Point.
Old range discontinued 15 November 1912 (LHF). Other records give 1922.
New offshore range named Bloody Point activated 15 November 1912 (LHF). Bulletin for 1912 lists a flashing change.
USLHS place record gives 1922 as discontinued.
Keeper's dwelling sold at public auction, 9 January 1922, to Francis Keenan (LHF).
Bought by Wick Scurry of Calibogue Cruises (hhi.com; LHF).

keepers.name: John M. Doyle
keepers.note: Principal keeper per the USLHS roster. LHF: appointed first caretaker 4 April 1883 at $620 a year; resigned 15 August 1890; had served with the Union Army as far south as Savannah (LHF). Also erected the tower with Cooper Manufacturing.

keepers.name: Robert A. Sisson
keepers.note: Succeeded Doyle (LHF). Keeper at the 1893 storm, per LHF's claim letter.

notes_for_editor: Read before publishing. Fact-checked 2026-10-28 (independent pass). Corrections made: (a) the paragraph headed 'In 1897' (scan p. 364, paragraph 683) is in the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1896 (printed 1897), not FY1897; source 15 and the story now say so. (b) The March 1895 item is a notice to mariners dated 5 March, not a Lighthouse Board notice. (c) The 1893 newspaper gives what the keeper told the paper; it is not his written account, and it does not name the keeper. (d) The 1922 auction paragraph no longer implies that LighthouseFriends dates the range's end to 1922 (it gives 15 Nov 1912; the USLHS front-range record gives 1922). (e) The roster citation now points to the place record (archives.uslhs.org/places/bloody-point-range-front), which prints the same keeper lines as the roster. (f) Source 15 is the FY1896 volume; the Commissioner 1916 list is scan p. 142 (printed p. 33), checked with corpus.py page. (g) Unreconciled, stated in the story: the 1900 narrative ('site of the rear beacon, about 1 mile distant') against the list of lights moved ('60 feet nearer rear light'); LighthouseFriends' 4,350 ft move; the rear tower, 91 ft in LighthouseFriends against 81 ft to the lantern in the USLHS rear record (24.7 m). (h) The 1912 Bulletin (PDF p. 47) gives the range as 'Ga.'; the OCR text was checked, the page image was not. (i) Secondary-only facts are paraphrased and attributed to LighthouseFriends or hhi.com (copyrighted sites): Doyle's Union Army service and role, the 1881 appropriation, the 1882 land deal, the 20 April 1883 first lighting, the 1908 engineer's report, the 1922 auction price, Ohman's and Burn's dates, the 2015 sale. The Board's 1883-1890 reports are not in the local corpus. (j) Wikipedia is not cited. (k) People: Papy Burn died in 1968 (LighthouseFriends) and is named in his public role; private owners between 1926 and 2015 are not named; Wick Scurry is named as operator of Calibogue Cruises, which runs the museum. (l) No photos were sourced; none were found in the sources read.
